Overall, we expect the iPhone 18 Pro will not have major upgrades compared to the previous generation. In fact, if you're currently using an older iPhone, there are actually plenty of reasons to buy an iPhone 17 Pro before next week's new model launch.

Among the few upgrades we expect, the biggest one on paper will be the variable aperture on the main camera. But in actual use, will this really make a noticeable difference…?

Variable aperture controls depth of field

One of the biggest differences between photos taken with a DSLR or mirrorless camera and those taken with an iPhone is the control over depth of field (DOF).

When using a traditional camera, a wide aperture can create shallow depth of field, most commonly used to separate the subject from the background. Portrait photos are the classic example (which is why Apple's simulated shallow depth of field effect is called "Portrait Mode").

Conversely, when shooting landscapes or cityscapes, a narrow aperture is usually used to ensure everything from foreground to background remains sharp and clear.

Therefore, variable aperture has always been a standard feature of any traditional camera lens. In contrast, the iPhone has always used a fixed aperture lens. (There are some ways to achieve shallow depth of field with an iPhone, which I'll cover in a separate article after the new models launch, but these are exceptions rather than the norm.)

iPhone lens gets variable aperture

We expect this year's iPhone to be the first to feature a variable aperture lens. It remains unclear whether this feature will be applied to both iPhone 18 Pro models, or limited to the Pro Max only. In any case, it's expected to be limited to the main lens, not the ultrawide or telephoto lens.

On paper, this is indeed big news. In theory, a variable aperture lens gives us control over depth of field. But in practice, we shouldn't get too excited about achieving the kind of effect shown in the large image at the top of this article—the reason is that some things won't change.

The bad news

The main limiting factor for the iPhone is not the lens aperture (the aperture itself is already quite large), but the size of the image sensor. All else being equal, the larger the sensor, the more pronounced the shallow depth of field effect can be. Compared to DSLRs and mirrorless cameras, the iPhone's sensor is much smaller, and that won't change this year.

With the same sensor size and only a slightly larger aperture, the laws of physics mean we shouldn't expect a huge difference.

Potential good news

That said, there may still be a glimmer of hope. Adding a mechanical variable aperture to one of the iPhone's lenses is no simple engineering feat. Given the compact size of the lens, this design is both complex and costly.

So we have to ask the question: why would Apple go to this trouble and expense to do something with fairly limited expected benefits? If the end result is just the degree of difference that calculations predict, it wouldn't really be worth doing.

This leads me to speculate—if Apple really plans to make this new feature a key selling point, there must be something more to it behind the scenes.

One possibility I can think of is that this optical upgrade is almost a cover for significant improvements to Portrait Mode. The simulated effect improves every year, but there's still room for improvement, perhaps with an upgraded chip's AI computing power allowing Apple to achieve more natural results?

If that's the case, I suspect most people won't mind it being a kind of "shortcut"—the variable aperture only brings marginal benefits, while the software improvements are what truly bring more significant improvements. For most people, what matters most is the final result. This is my best guess for now.

Have a better idea? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
